subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a cross of two heterozygous black guinea pigs (Bb x Bb) where black is dominant to white, the probability that a single offspring is white is:
questions.explain: Bb x Bb gives a 3:1 ratio, so each offspring has a 1 in 4 chance of being homozygous recessive (white).

questions.q: Haemophilia is more common in males than females because:
options: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome
questions.explain: The recessive allele is X-linked, and males (XY) express it with only one copy as they have no second X to mask it.

questions.q: A man with blood group O (genotype ii) and a woman with group AB (IAIB) have children. The possible blood groups of their children are:
questions.explain: Each child receives i from the father and either IA or IB from the mother, giving group A or group B only.

questions.q: A condition occurs in 1 in 10 000 people and is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the recessive allele frequency (q) is:
questions.explain: q squared = 1/10 000 = 0.0001, so q = the square root of 0.0001 = 0.01.

questions.q: A producer has a GPP of 20,000 kJ per m2 per yr and respiratory losses of 8,000 kJ per m2 per yr. What is its NPP?
questions.explain: NPP = GPP - respiration = 20,000 - 8,000 = 12,000 kJ per m2 per yr.

questions.q: Which equation correctly expresses net primary productivity (NPP)?
questions.explain: NPP is the energy left for growth after the producers' respiratory losses are subtracted from GPP.

questions.q: In the biological species concept, two organisms belong to the same species if they can:
questions.explain: The biological species concept defines a species as a group able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

questions.q: Crossing over between linked genes during meiosis produces:
options: Recombinant offspring with new allele combinations
questions.explain: Crossing over swaps alleles between homologous chromosomes, generating recombinant combinations among linked genes.

questions.q: Directional selection is characterised by:
options: Both extremes being favoured over the mean
The population mean shifting towards one extreme phenotype
questions.explain: Directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the population mean in that direction over time.

questions.q: A genetic bottleneck reduces genetic diversity because:
options: A sharp fall in population size leaves only a small, less varied sample of alleles
questions.explain: A bottleneck drastically reduces numbers, so surviving individuals carry only a fraction of the original variation.

questions.q: During succession, how does each community typically change the environment?
options: It makes conditions less suitable for itself but more suitable for the next community
It reduces biodiversity at every stage
questions.explain: Each stage alters the abiotic conditions, often making them less suitable for itself but enabling new species to colonise.

questions.q: Comparing the base sequence of DNA or amino acid sequences of proteins helps classification because more closely related species:
options: Show fewer differences in their base or amino acid sequences
questions.explain: Closely related species have had less time to accumulate sequence differences, so they are more similar.

questions.q: The maximum population size an environment can support sustainably is known as the:
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population an ecosystem's resources can support over a long period.

questions.q: A test cross of a heterozygote with a homozygous recessive individual is expected to give a phenotypic ratio of:
questions.explain: Crossing Aa with aa yields half Aa and half aa, a 1:1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.q: Genetic drift differs from natural selection because drift:
options: Changes allele frequencies by chance rather than by differential survival
Cannot remove alleles from a population
questions.explain: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, unrelated to the alleles' effects on fitness.

questions.q: What is a deflected succession (plagioclimax)?
options: The earliest pioneer stage of succession
A succession that reaches its natural climax community
A community held at a stage before the natural climax by human activity such as grazing
questions.explain: Continued human or animal interference, such as grazing or mowing, stops succession reaching its natural climax.

questions.q: In a pyramid of energy, why is each successive trophic level smaller, and why is a pyramid of energy never inverted?
options: Energy increases up the food chain
Energy is lost at each transfer, so less is always available to the next level
Energy is created at each level
questions.explain: Because energy is lost as heat and in unconsumed material at every transfer, each level always has less energy than the one below.

questions.q: A low index of diversity in a habitat suggests an ecosystem that is:
options: Highly stable and resistant to change
Dominated by few species and more vulnerable to environmental change
questions.explain: Low diversity indicates few species or uneven abundance, making the ecosystem less stable and more vulnerable.

questions.q: In epistasis, when a recessive allele at one locus in the homozygous state prevents expression of a second gene, this is termed:
questions.explain: Recessive epistasis occurs when the homozygous recessive genotype at one locus masks the second gene's expression.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the greatest effect on allele frequencies in:
options: Small populations, where chance events strongly affect allele frequencies
questions.explain: In small populations, random chance (drift) can cause large fluctuations in allele frequencies between generations.

questions.q: Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are reproductively isolated by:
options: A behavioural difference within the same area
A change in mating season only
A geographical barrier such as a mountain or river
questions.explain: In allopatric speciation a physical/geographical barrier separates populations, allowing them to diverge.

questions.q: For the mark-release-recapture method to give a valid estimate, which assumption must hold?
options: Marking does not affect survival and marked individuals mix randomly with the population
questions.explain: The estimate assumes marks are harmless and that marked individuals redistribute randomly before the second sample.

questions.q: A geneticist obtains a chi-squared value with a probability (p) of 0.30 that the deviation is due to chance. The correct conclusion is to:
options: Accept the null hypothesis as the deviation is not significant
questions.explain: As p is greater than 0.05, the deviation is not significant, so the null hypothesis is accepted.

questions.q: How does secondary succession differ from primary succession?
options: It involves no change in species over time
It never reaches a climax community
It begins on land that already has soil, e.g. after a fire
It begins on bare rock with no soil
questions.explain: Secondary succession starts where soil already exists, so it proceeds faster than primary succession.

questions.q: Which of the following is a density-dependent factor affecting population size?
options: Competition for food as the population grows
questions.explain: Competition intensifies as density rises, so its effect depends on population density, unlike abiotic events.

questions.q: For a chi-squared test on a dihybrid cross with four phenotypic classes, the number of degrees of freedom is:
questions.explain: Degrees of freedom equal the number of categories minus one, so 4 - 1 = 3.

questions.q: In a Hardy-Weinberg population, the equation p + q = 1 represents the sum of:
options: The two allele frequencies for a gene with two alleles
questions.explain: p and q are the frequencies of the two alleles, which must add up to 1.

questions.q: The ABO blood group system is an example of multiple alleles because:
options: There are more than two alleles in the population for one gene
Each person has more than two alleles
questions.explain: Three alleles (IA, IB, i) exist in the population for the single ABO gene, though each individual carries only two.

questions.q: Which process in the nitrogen cycle returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere, reducing soil fertility?
questions.explain: Denitrifying bacteria in anaerobic soils convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, lowering soil nitrogen.

questions.q: During primary succession, what is the key role of the pioneer species?
options: They prevent any further species from establishing
They form the stable climax community
They are the top predators of the food web
They colonise bare rock and begin soil formation
questions.explain: Pioneers such as lichens colonise inhospitable bare surfaces and start building soil for later species.
